beats.script_body: A Sunday morning full of wind and sunlight. Over the large pool the wind splatters the waters of the fountains, the tiny sailboats on the windswept water, and the swallows around the huge trees — Albert Camus recorded the scene in his Notebooks. Having borne witness to the life of Paris for almost four hundred years, the Luxembourg's pleasures embody the beauty of that life: symmetrical rows of chestnut trees, in April the pretty beds of tulips, the murmur of so many people relaxing in the sun, children jubilant before the puppet theater, then hunched over the rim of the large central octagonal basin intent on their sailboats, and above them in the shade of the gazebo on the eastern terrace, the conviviality of music and wine and the company of friends.

key_claims: Luxembourg Gardens has borne witness to Paris life for almost 400 years

beats.script_body: The Fontaine Médicis in the northeast corner of the Luxembourg Gardens is an Italian Renaissance gem of the 1620s, built for the Florentine Marie de Médicis — queen and then widow of Henri IV. Paris despised her; in the words of André Maurois, she was "a haughty Italian — a fat blonde, handsome enough when Rubens painted her, very well pleased with herself, an authoritarian without authority." But the fountain is Marie's legacy. The stillness of the pool, shadowed by a surround of arching plane trees, contrasts with the mad narrative of the fountain sculpture: the mythological Polyphemus, the gigantic Cyclops and jealous suitor, menacing the lovers Acis and Galatea, as if poised to devour them.

beats.script_body: The Luxembourg Palace was Marie de Médicis's attempt to re-create her hometown in this foreign city — she had the Pitti Palace in Florence in mind. Though no longer open to the public, the palace is built on ground where the Romans once set up their military camp, and is now the proud house of the French Senate.

beats.script_body: The Luxembourg Palace has two dark chapters written into its walls. In the Paris Commune of 1871, government troops dumped the corpses of Communards in the surrounding shrubbery. During the German Occupation from 1940 to 1944, the palace served as the headquarters of the Luftwaffe and the SS — and yet Nazi gardeners kept the lovely flower gardens bordering it groomed and flourishing. In August 1944, as Allied and French troops fought to take back Paris, seven hundred Germans ready to "fight to the last cartridge" dug trenches and hid tanks in the beds of geraniums and begonias. From the roof and cupola they tracked the approaching regiments. The Luxembourg Palace was the last German stronghold in Paris to surrender. When it finally did, on August 25th, "formally and definitively, Paris was free."

beats.script_body: First in line on the western terrace stands Laure de Noves (1307–1348) — serenely self-possessed, holding a book in her sleeve. She was neither queen nor saint, but the muse of Petrarch: the woman he first saw at Mass in a church in Aquitaine, the inspiration of his sonnets, the Canzoniere. She had married into the de Sade family. More than four centuries later, in his prison cell at Vincennes, her descendant the mad Marquis de Sade dreamed of Laure as his ancestral idol: "Her eyes had the same fire as when Petrarch sang of them. . . . I am like a child. I flung myself at her feet, calling, 'Oh, my mother!'"

beats.script_body: Walking east of the eastern terrace near the Saint-Michel entrance, you pass a statue of George Sand — novelist, passionately unconventional. She was admired by Flaubert, Matthew Arnold, the Brownings, Charlotte Brontë, George Eliot, Heinrich Heine, Turgenev, and Proust. Oscar Wilde loved her for her compassion and generosity: "For the aristocracy of the intellect she had always the deepest veneration, but the democracy of suffering touched her more."

beats.script_body: West of the western terrace you pass the Luxembourg regulars, for whom the word "leisure" is not an abstraction: the chess players near the Orangerie, the men on the boules courts, the children on the carousel, the readers who are everywhere. You get a sense of down-to-earth practical wisdom, of the arts of survival that have seen Parisians through centuries of wars and suffering. In the Luxembourg, the tough complex soul of the city comes through.

beats.script_body: Turning left off rue de l'Abbaye into a corner of the serene Place de Furstemberg, you find the apartment and studio — now a museum — of the sublime French painter Eugène Delacroix (1798–1863). Delacroix moved here from the Right Bank in 1857 so he could walk back and forth to Saint-Sulpice, where his murals had been commissioned for the Chapelle des Saints-Anges — the Chapel of the Holy Angels. "I like my studio," he confided to his journal. "I work well here. The view from my small garden . . . always gives me pleasure." In this silent retreat, sitting under the trees, he planned his last masterpieces.

beats.script_body: The museum's small shaded garden with benches is a delightful place to sit and read The Journal of Eugène Delacroix — on sale in the bookshop, and described by editor Hubert Wellington as "perhaps the greatest literary testament any painter has left." The journal illuminates Delacroix's passion for the beauty of the world and the medium of his art: he writes about mixing colors, how to achieve specific effects, his excitement at the sight of his palette. He notes the pleasures of the Luxembourg Gardens, where he studies the shapes of leaves and trees, and records his visits to the Jardins des Plantes to watch the animals in the Natural History museum.

beats.script_body: Although Delacroix's health had been poor, he told his friend George Sand that his work at Saint-Sulpice had given back the health he thought lost forever: "I get up very early and hurry off to my work. I return home as late as possible and begin again the next day. . . . Nothing gives me more pleasure than painting. . . . I am buried in my work." He did not mourn the loss of his social life — the nightly dinner parties, concerts, and openings in the company of his friends Baudelaire, Balzac, Corot, Berlioz, Mérimée, Madame Sand, and his beloved Chopin (1810–1849).

beats.script_body: Delacroix's journal captures the torment and ecstasy of creation: "What a good life! What a divine compensation for my solitary state. . . . Painting, it's true, like the most exacting of mistresses, harasses and torments me in a hundred ways. . . . I have been getting up at dawn, and hurrying off to this enchanting work as though I were rushing to throw myself at the feet of a beloved mistress. . . . How is it that this unending struggle revives instead of destroying me!" Among his paintings, the most famous is Liberty Guiding the People, commemorating the uprising of July 28, 1830 — it hangs in the Louvre, as well as in the Musée du Petit Palais and the Musée d'Orsay.

beats.source_passage: What a good life! What a divine compensation for my solitary state. . . . Painting, its true, like the most exacting of mistresses, harasses and torments me in a hundred ways. ... I have been getting up at dawn, and hurrying off to this enchanting work as though I were rushing to throw myself at the feet of a beloved mistress. . . . How is it that this unending struggle revives instead of destroying me! Reading Delacroix, you want to see both his Paris and his paintings, many of which, including the most famous—Liberty Guiding the People, commemorating the uprising of July 28, 1830—hang in the Louvre as well as in the Musee du Petit Palais and the Musee d'Orsay.

beats.script_body: Inside this small uncrowded museum you find powerful evidence of Delacroix's genius for dramatizing color in works suffused with love for women subjects: Jenny Le Guillou, Magdalen au Désert, Éducation de la Vierge, a drawing of George Sand. There are also works devoted to the sea, to landscape — La Nuit ou l'Inondation — and to wild animals, including the Bacchus Fresco. But it is outside, in the stillness of the garden, where the visitor may best contemplate the reveries of this romantic visionary. "God is within us," he writes on October 12, 1862. "He is the inner presence that causes us to admire the beautiful."

beats.script_body: Simone de Beauvoir studied mathematics at the Institut Catholique, and the philosopher Jacques Maritain taught philosophy here. Stranded in the United States during the Occupation, Maritain taught at Princeton and wrote France My Country (1941), a love letter to Paris: "How did it fall, this city of our hopes, this country that taught liberty to the world?"

beats.script_body: The tower of Saint-Germain-des-Prés dominates the Place — the familiar image of the Romanesque origin of what remains of a huge Benedictine monastery from the sixth century. The transition from Romanesque to early Gothic is evident in the interior. The marble statue Notre-Dame de Consolation, given to the Abbey of Saint-Denis in 1340, stands in the rear of the south aisle. Fragments from the Lady Chapel (1212–1255) are scattered outside next to the church entrance in the garden of Square Laurent-Prâghe, where Picasso's Head of a Woman also stands.

beats.source_passage: THE CHURCH OF SAINT-GERMAIN-DES-PRES (Saint-Germain of the Fields) Open daily 8—y. The tower dominates the Place, the familiar image of the Romanesque origin of what remains of a huge Benedictine monastery from the sixth century. The transition from Romanesque to early Gothic is evident in the interior, a beautiful setting for the concerts held here and posted outside. The marble statue, Notre-Dame de Consolation, given to the Abbey of Saint-Denis in 1340, stands in the rear of the south aisle. Fragments from the Lady Chapel (1212—1255) are scattered outside next to the church entrance in the garden of Square Laurent-Praghe, where Picasso's Head of a Woman also stands.
